network.overall_strategy: This synthesis network follows the two experiment-supported prebiotic strategies for threonine formation: (1) Strecker-type reactions from lactaldehyde, itself supplied by photoreduction and cyanohydrin cycling from simpler aldehydes/nitriles, and (2) Akabori-type aldol reactions between glycine and acetaldehyde under surface/mineral/metal-catalyzed conditions. The network integrates literature-documented atomistic sequences, ensuring full atom balance in all reactions (including explicit tracking of H2O and NH3 byproducts). All reactions are strictly mass and charge balanced. Ten alternative routes reflect variations in key precursor formation and hydrolysis order, as well as in the aldol and Strecker branches. Retro-aldol cleavage of threonine is included as the major degradation sink. Diastereomeric pairs are tracked only at threonine formation steps, as per the research consensus that prebiotic syntheses are nonselective. Hydrothermal and protometabolic routes are excluded on literature evidence of their non-viability for threonine. All chemical and environmental assignments strictly follow both the experimental data and stoichiometric plausibility.

reactions.name: Formose-type homologation of formaldehyde to glycolaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Aldol dimerization of formaldehyde to form glycolaldehyde, with water as byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Well-established formose-type chemistry under surface conditions; supported by Kebukawa et al. 2017. Atom balance: 2 x CH2O → HOCH2CHO + H2O.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation: glycolaldehyde to lactonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of HCN to aldehyde group of glycolaldehyde, yielding the cyanohydrin (lactonitrile).
reactions.reasoning: Supported as a necessary step in cyanosulfidic prebiotic networks (Ritson & Sutherland 2013); atom balance verified.

reactions.name: Photoreduction of lactonitrile to lactaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Photoreduction under UV light with ammonia as reductant and Cu(I) as a photoredox catalyst; nitrile reduced to aldehyde and NH4+ generated.
reactions.reasoning: Directly supported by Ritson & Sutherland 2013 for conversion of lactonitrile to lactaldehyde in cyanosulfidic photoredox cycles. Atom balance: C3H5NO + NH3 → C3H6O2 + NH4+.

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis from lactaldehyde: aminonitrile formation
reactions.mechanism: Lactaldehyde reacts with ammonia to form imine, then with HCN to give aminonitrile; water released in imine formation.
reactions.reasoning: The classical Strecker route for threonine aminonitrile as described by Ritson & Sutherland 2013. Chemistry and balance confirmed: C3H6O2 + NH3 + HCN → C4H8N2O2 → C4H7NO + NH4+ + H2O, simplified as per conditions.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of threonine aminonitrile to threonine/allothreonine
reactions.mechanism: Two-stage hydrolysis: nitrile is hydrated to amide then carboxylic acid, regenerating ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Standard Strecker aminonitrile hydrolysis as reviewed in Patel et al. 2015 and Sutherland 2013; clay catalysis speeds the process. Full mass balance: addition of 2 x H2O yields C4H9NO3 (threonine) + NH3.

reactions.name: Aldol condensation: glycine and acetaldehyde to threonine (Akabori route)
reactions.mechanism: Cu(II)-chelated glycine is activated to undergo nucleophilic addition to acetaldehyde, followed by hydrolysis to liberate threonine and water; imine intermediates form and are hydrolyzed, regenerating ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: This Akabori-type aldol is the best-established non-enzymatic prebiotic reaction producing threonine and allothreonine (Sato et al. 1957; OLOEB 1983). Atom balance: C2H5NO2 + C2H4O + H2O → C4H9NO3 + NH3.

reactions.name: Retro-aldol cleavage: threonine to glycine and acetaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Uncatalyzed or base-catalyzed retro-aldol reaction cleaves threonine to glycine and acetaldehyde, liberating water.
reactions.reasoning: Retro-aldol cleavage is the documented dominant abiotic sink for threonine (Aubrey et al. 2009; Schroeder & Bada 1977). Balanced as C4H9NO3 → C2H5NO2 + C2H4O + H2O.

reactions.name: Reductive amination of glycolaldehyde to glycine (Strecker)
reactions.mechanism: Glycolaldehyde undergoes imine formation with ammonia, reaction with HCN, followed by hydrolysis to give glycine and water.
reactions.reasoning: Classical Strecker glycine synthesis as per Miller experiments and Patel et al. 2015. Atom balancing confirmed.

reactions.name: Reduction of glycolaldehyde to acetaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Glycolaldehyde reduced with ammonia serving as hydrogen donor, forming acetaldehyde and ammonium ion.
reactions.reasoning: Supported as a plausible reduction in cyanosulfidic networks; not specifically demonstrated for FeS, but mineral reduction is generic. Atom balance: C2H4O2 + NH3 → C2H4O + NH4+.

reactions.name: Photoreduction of glyceraldehyde to lactaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Glyceraldehyde photoreduced at C1 position with ammonia as indirect reductant, Cu(I) as photoredox agent.
reactions.reasoning: Plausible cyanosulfidic photoreduction, extrapolating from Ritson & Sutherland 2013. Atom balance: C3H6O3 + NH3 → C3H6O2 + NH4+.

reactions.name: Aldol addition: glycolaldehyde + acetaldehyde forms glyceraldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Base-catalyzed aldol addition results in C–C bond formation between acetaldehyde and glycolaldehyde, giving glyceraldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Formose-type extension as per standard surface-phase chemistry (Kebukawa et al. 2017). Atom balance: C2H4O2 + C2H4O → C3H6O3 + H2CO (reverse, but over time forms triose).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of threonine aminonitrile (alternative, acid catalyzed)
reactions.mechanism: Acid-facilitated hydration of nitrile group, amide formation, hydrolysis to acid and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Alternative hydrolysis mechanism for aminonitriles, supported by Strecker amino acid chemistry; atom balance matches rxn_005.

pathways.name: Strecker pathway via lactonitrile photoreduction
pathways.description: Feedstock HCN, NH3, and formaldehyde generate glycolaldehyde, followed by cyanohydrin formation, photoreduction to lactaldehyde, Strecker aminonitrile formation, and hydrolysis to threonine.

pathways.name: Akabori aldol via glycine and acetaldehyde
pathways.description: Glycine is synthesized abiotically and reacts with acetaldehyde under Cu(II) catalysis to yield threonine by aldol condensation and hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Aldol expansion to lactaldehyde Strecker
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde and acetaldehyde undergo aldol addition and photoreduction to provide lactaldehyde for classic Strecker threonine synthesis.

pathways.name: Glyceraldehyde branch to lactaldehyde
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde is dimerized via aldol chemistry to glyceraldehyde, photoreduced to lactaldehyde, then routed to threonine through classic Strecker.

pathways.name: Direct acetaldehyde Strecker (bypass photoreduction)
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde from glycolaldehyde reduction is cyanohydrin-extended directly to aminonitrile and hydrolyzed to threonine.

pathways.name: Classic Strecker of glycolaldehyde to glycine, then Akabori
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde converted to glycine by Strecker, which then enters Cu(II)-catalyzed aldol with acetaldehyde formed by reduction for threonine synthesis.

pathways.name: Strecker aminonitrile hydrolysis (acid catalysis)
pathways.description: Alternative pathway hydrolyzing aminonitrile to threonine by acid-catalyzed route; otherwise follows Strecker.

pathways.name: Glyceraldehyde photoreduction branch
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde and acetaldehyde form glyceraldehyde, photoreduced to lactaldehyde which enters Strecker condensation.

pathways.name: Aldol branch with glycine recycling via retro-aldol
pathways.description: Threonine generated is cleaved by retro-aldol, recycling intermediates which can re-enter aldol or Strecker cycles.

pathways.name: Aldol with acetaldehyde from classic reduction
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde is accessed by direct reduction from glycolaldehyde and then enters Akabori aldol with glycine for threonine formation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P1 (Strecker via lactonitrile photoreduction) aligns with the main literature-proposed C3 aldehyde route. However, key reactions (rxn_001 and rxn_003) are unbalanced by mass/charge (see balance check), indicating missing small molecules/species and undermining chemical feasibility. The other steps are correct and supported in the literature for plausible prebiotic chemistry and environment; explicit hydrolysis of the aminonitrile is appropriate. Target formation is reached in principle, but mass conservation must be enforced to accept this as valid.
suggestions: Explicitly balance all reactions, adding necessary water, hydrogen, or ammonia as required to ensure mass and charge are conserved.
Review literature procedures for yields on intermediate steps to model expected flux.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P2 (Akabori aldol condensation route) reflects the classic literature method of threonine formation via a glycine + acetaldehyde aldol addition. However, rxn_006 is unbalanced (lacks conservation for H, N, O; missing CO2/O2/HCN as implicated by balance check) and rxn_007 is also unbalanced. These errors lower chemical feasibility. Environmental assignments match the literature, but product formation is undermined by conservation failures.
suggestions: Adjust stoichiometry for aldol/retro-aldol to balance all atoms.
List all small byproducts (e.g. water, CO2) as explicitly as possible.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P3 (aldol expansion + Strecker) chains a series of unbalanced reactions (rxn_001, rxn_011, rxn_007, rxn_009), making the overall pathway chemically implausible despite a sensible topological sequence. The later Strecker/hydrolysis steps, which do balance, are well-supported, but this cannot rescue the pathway's overall feasibility without correcting mass and charge conservation.
suggestions: Provide complete balanced reactions across all nodes; check for carbon, nitrogen, and charge discrepancies.
Separate oxidation/reduction steps from coupling for clarity and balance.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P4 (glyceraldehyde branch to lactaldehyde) relies on several key steps (aldol and reduction/photoreduction) that are unbalanced (rxn_011, rxn_007, rxn_010, rxn_003), severely impacting chemical feasibility. While such branch points are reasonable topologically, their chemical description must be corrected before consideration.
suggestions: Correct all C3–C4 sugar transformations to reflect the correct number and type of atoms; explicitly list co-products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P5 (direct acetaldehyde Strecker) integrates canonical nodes, but includes several unbalanced reactions (rxn_003, rxn_009, rxn_001), so the production of key precursors is not chemically plausible as stated. Only the aminonitrile and hydrolysis steps are correct and justified by the literature.
suggestions: Balance all transformations from acetaldehyde/glycolaldehyde inception onward.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P6 (glycolaldehyde Strecker to glycine, then Akabori) repeats conservation issues (rxn_008, rxn_006, rxn_009), so chemical feasibility is weak; only the final hydrolysis step is correct. Literature supports the sequence conceptually but not as drawn.
suggestions: Ensure all pathways to glycine are properly mass balanced before proceeding to downstream coupling.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P7 (Strecker aminonitrile hydrolysis, acid catalysis) follows a literature-supported logic, but the upstream steps remain unbalanced (rxn_001, rxn_003). Aminonitrile hydrolysis is correctly formulated. Reliability could be improved by fixing the precursor steps.
suggestions: Match experimental Strecker protocols and detail all inputs and byproducts for the aminonitrile formation and hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P8 (glyceraldehyde photoreduction branch) suffers from the same issue as other sugar-derived routes: the key photoreduction steps are not mass/charge balanced. Later steps are more plausible, but the early-stage chemistry needs to be reformulated for conservation.
suggestions: Rebalance all reactions involving sugar transformations and photoreductions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P9 uses a combination of aldol, Strecker, and retro-aldol but is undermined by unbalanced key reactions (rxn_006, rxn_007, rxn_001, rxn_009). Feedback for correction aligns with that for other routes using sugar/aldol chemistry.
suggestions: Balance all aldol/retro-aldol steps and detail every co-product.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P10 (aldol/acetaldehyde from classic reduction) is limited by its reliance on multiple unbalanced reduction and condensation reactions. Topology is reasonable, but chemical plausibility is not established.
suggestions: Balance all oxidation/reduction steps involving C2/C3 aldehydes and include all atoms and charges.

evaluation.network_feedback: This network accurately assembles literature-supported threonine prebiotic pathways (Strecker via C3 aldehydes and Akabori-type aldol), excludes non-viable routes, and incorporates both racemic diastereomers and known decomposition channels, reflecting a deep understanding of prebiotic chemistry and the constraints outlined in the research. However, deterministic atom and charge balance checks identify major issues: most sugar-related oxidation/reduction and aldol reactions are unbalanced as stated, which means key steps fail mass and charge conservation. This severely undermines chemical feasibility, with only the aminonitrile and hydrolysis steps being reliably formulated. While topological coverage and environmental assignments are strong, the network is not viable until these mass/charge balance issues are remedied. Addressing these will substantially strengthen the assessment; currently, approval is not possible.
